children: By Lila MacLellan
When Ron Shaich's father was close to dying, he had a revelation: He had messed up in life, making poorly considered decisions and living impulsively.

Shaich, the Panera co-founder and former CEO who now runs Act III Holdings-an investment group that owns major stakes in Cava and the smaller Tatte Bakery & Café chain, among other businesses-told me about the impact of his father's death when we met at Manhattan's first Tatte location yesterday.

"If you have a chronic illness, there's a judgment day. That judgment day is the last months of your life when you look back," he said. His mother had died at peace with her life's decisions years before his father's passing, a contrast he reflects on in his book, "Know What Matters." And the divergence between his parents' experiences decades ago still informs the way he lives and operates. That is, with a view toward a final retrospective.   "First, I started doing it personally," he said. He'd ask, "Where do I want to be in three years in terms of my work, my family, my health, my relationship with my body, my relationship with my spirituality?"  "And then I began to say, 'Let's do that for a business. And every business that I'm in.'"

That was the beginning of a playbook that Shaich has used since growing Panera into a nationwide chain. (He sold Panera in 2017 in a $7.5 billion deal.) Today, his initial question at every Cava board meeting is still, "What is it that in three years you're going to wish we had dealt with today?" The idea is also core to the advice he has shared with CEOs who've come to him seeking guidance.

"I'm not sure it's different than children," Shaich said. "When you bring up children, so much of your energy is reacting to 'Oh, he's sick. Oh, he's this. Oh, he's that,'" but what matters is your longer-term influence on this developing person.

CEOs know that companies need to establish priorities, of course. But Shaich said he's found that they usually end up spending most of their time in a reactive mode anyway. When they do set priorities, he said, they often fail to drill down far enough; they don't set meaningful deadlines and define what success looks or feels like. Novice CEOs rarely surround themselves with the right "load-bearing" people who have specializations and can take ownership of specific goals. Instead, many try to take responsibility for everything.
Then again, working with CEOs and asking them really tough questions to help them deal with all of this is what keeps him in the business at age 72, he said. "I love figuring it out."

By the way, as a parent, Shaich apparently isn't above responding to arguably trivial issues. When his adult son who happened to be working at Tatte stopped by with a question, Shaich zeroed in on a shadow of stubble he spotted. (The family had attended the record-breakingly long U.S. Open game the night before.) Then he responded with his own question: "We don't shave anymore?"
Lila MacLellan Editor, CEO Brief
